# Summary: Education in Sweden
Sweden's education system comprises a nine-year compulsory comprehensive school (grundskola) for children aged approximately 7 to 16, divided into lower, middle, and upper stages. Education starts with optional preschool (förskola) from age one, with free attendance from age three for at least three hours daily; preschool class (förskoleklass) is for 6–7-year-olds and precedes compulsory schooling. The compulsory grundskola offers 16 core subjects throughout all nine grades, including Swedish, mathematics, sciences, English, technology, arts, and physical education. From grade 6, students receive grades (A-F), and national tests in grades 3, 6, and 9 assess proficiency in core subjects to ensure grading consistency. Approximately 15.6% of students leaving compulsory school do not qualify for upper secondary education, mostly boys and those with foreign backgrounds.
Upper secondary education (gymnasieskola), usually lasting three years for students aged 16–19, offers 18 national programmes divided into preparatory academic tracks (two-thirds of students) and vocational tracks. Admission is competitive and based on grundskola grades, with eligibility requiring passing key subjects including Swedish, English, and mathematics. All students must complete a diploma project. Students not meeting requirements for national programmes can enroll in introductory programmes, often for immigrants or those needing to improve core skills.
Higher education follows the Bologna framework, offering bachelor’s (3 years), master’s (1–2 years), and doctoral degrees (3–4 years) at universities and university colleges. Admission requires completion of upper secondary education. Tuition is free for Swedish, EU/EEA, and Swiss citizens; others usually pay fees. Grading varies by institution but includes a common European Credit Transfer and Accumulation System (ECTS) equivalence. Students may also take the SweSAT aptitude test for university admission. Since the 1990s, independent publicly funded “free schools” (friskolor) have expanded, including private, religious, and alternative pedagogy schools, now enrolling over 10% of pupils. These schools receive public funding but cannot charge fees or select pupils by examination. The independent school system is politically contentious, with debates on profit limits and religious education.
Sweden participates actively in equitable and quality education efforts. National assessments (PISA and PIRLS) showed declines between 2006 and 2012 with some recovery thereafter. Challenges include grade inflation especially in independent schools, disparities linked to immigration, methodological issues in testing, and increasing reports of school violence. Guidelines on violence and armed incidents have been issued in response to rising reports. Overall, Sweden’s education system is characterized by comprehensive compulsory schooling, diverse upper secondary options, free higher education, and a balance between public and independently run schools within a centralized framework.
